prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active forms, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: All six openings place B033 first, and I still think that is the correct reading of the evidence rather than a convenient consensus. The achievement runs from gut-hormone physiology (the incretin effect, proglucagon processing, the identity and secretion of the active truncated GLP-1 forms, receptor biology) to drug classes with large randomized outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. Originality, clarity of mechanism, breadth of patient impact and maturity are all strong, and the physiology is what a Physiology or Medicine prize is meant to reward. I favour crediting the three basic-science contributors, Holst, Drucker and Mojsov, because the three-person limit forces a choice and the physiology is the discovery, while the industrial development is the application of it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. Mojsov's priority relative to Habener and colleagues is contested and I cannot resolve it from the supplied record, and leaving out Knudsen, whose medicinal chemistry produced liraglutide and semaglutide, means the prize honours the mechanism but not the molecules that reached patients. If the committee judges that the clinical transformation is the achievement, a physiology-only trio is vulnerable to the criticism that it omits the people most directly responsible for the medicines. My preference also rests on my recollection of the priority history, which I have not verified here.

responses.point: Sten ranks B032 (BCR-ABL inhibition in CML) second, arguing that Lydon, Druker and Sawyers form a natural trio, that the paradigm of targeted kinase inhibition is fully confirmed over decades, and that recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I take the maturity argument seriously, since durable survival in CML is as clear a clinical result as any on the list. My qualification is that the prize-defining insight, that an oncogenic kinase can be a drug target, rests on BCR-ABL and Philadelphia chromosome work outside the credited names, so the trio rewards drug discovery and clinical proof rather than the underlying biology. GLP-1 gives a cleaner physiology-to-therapy chain with the discovery itself inside the credited group. I would keep B032 as a credible alternative but I do not rank it above B033, and I would not rank it above CAR-T on conceptual novelty.

responses.point: Marie puts B051 (anti-TNF therapy, Feldmann and Maini) second, as a clean two-person configuration with the principle of cytokine-targeted therapy in chronic autoimmune disease, two decades of use and a stable field.
responses.response: The two-person attribution is indeed cleaner than in most entries, and the concept of a single cytokine as a dominant driver of chronic inflammation is important. My reservation is about newness of the achievement for a 2026 prize. Anti-TNF is the template for later biologics, but its impact on outcomes and its mechanistic elegance seem to me smaller than for incretin biology or engineered T cells, and the antibody engineering and TNF biology behind it involve many contributors beyond the pair. I would not oppose it in a two-part prize, but I do not see it displacing B033 or B026.

responses.point: Thomas favours the three basic-science GLP-1 contributors and, for CAR-T, June and Sadelain only, ranking antisense correction of SMN2 splicing (B045, Krainer and Bennett) third as a clean two-person pairing with clear mechanism and clinical outcome.
responses.response: I agree on the GLP-1 trio and on limiting CAR-T to June and Sadelain. On B045 I accept that nusinersen converted a lethal infant motor neuron disease into a treatable one and that the splicing mechanism is original, and as a neuroscientist I recognise the clinical significance. But the pairing credits mechanism and platform, while the clinical development involved others, and the long-term evidence is shorter than for B033 or B026. I would rank it as a strong but somewhat early candidate, not a first-tier one. Our disagreement is about timing more than merit.

responses.point: Per ranks B007 (optogenetics) third, describing it as an original and very widely used tool for causal tests of circuit function, but a method more than a disease mechanism, and noting that the three-person limit forces exclusion of Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck.
responses.response: I agree with the characterisation and I tried to weigh B007 as I would a candidate from any other field, not by familiarity. Its impact on experimental neuroscience is large, but a method prize here has to deal with a real attribution problem, since Nagel and Hegemann, Deisseroth, Boyden, Bamberg and Miesenböck each have defensible claims and any trio is contestable. Clinical translation is also still at an early stage. That makes it a good alternative but weaker than B033, where a three-name allocation is more defensible.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution should be credited alongside, or in place of, Habener and colleagues who are outside the supplied names.
Whether the committee will want to reward the drug-development contribution (Knudsen) instead of or in addition to the physiology.
Whether a two-part prize (for example GLP-1 combined with CAR-T) would be preferable to a single GLP-1 prize, given that this would force a reduction of the credited names to three in total.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate is apparent from my provided profile. The documented connections are a 2019 Physiological Reviews synthesis with Sten Grillner, collaboration with Patrik Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons. None involves a credited name on the shortlist, and Perlmann is a fellow committee member, not a candidate.
